💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in.
  • On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War patch.
  • Sources indicate that the Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in.

On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War patch. Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile.

Sources indicate that the Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times. Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. Russia began using the technique to support long-range drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.

During the Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Strait Bridge, the flying mesh network allowed operators located more than 250 kilometers away (155 miles) to remotely guide missiles and drones in evading Russian air defenses while also homing in on the bridge’s weakest structural points, according to the Financial Times.

According to recent reports, ukraine’s takedown of the bridge segment was preceded by weeks of preparatory strikes that systematically destroyed or degraded Russian air defense weapons, radars, and electronic warfare equipment arrayed to protect the bridge. The November 15 night attack on the bridge also coincided with the largest Ukrainian overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the full-scale war, Reuters reported.

Notably, Ukraine conducted the coordinated strike with primarily Ukrainian developed or adapted technologies. The Financial Times reported that “Ukrainian units involved in the operation deliberately avoided using Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink satellite network,” because of recent US restrictions that prevent Ukraine from using Starshield on drones or anything else traveling more than 100 miles per hour (161 kilometers per hour).

Recent findings suggest that ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that the latest US-imposed restrictions on Starshield have not yet been lifted, although SpaceX denied that the restrictions had returned. Zelenskyy described the speed limit as interfering with some Ukrainian drone interceptor technologies that were designed to defend against Russian drones attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.

It has been revealed that however, the Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Strait Bridge provide yet another example of how the Ukrainian military and defense technology companies have been learning to fight without relying on Starlink. This is also not the first time that Ukraine, arguably the leading country in developing latest battlefield uses of drones, has adopted a Russian battlefield innovation for its own uses.

In a recent development, from Russia’s view, the only glimmer of good news was that the bridge’s railway section survived the initial strikes. Ukrainian newspaper the Kyiv Independent pointed to Russian news and video sources indicating that trains appeared to be running again on the bridge on November 18.

Recent findings suggest that but Ukraine targeted the railway section yet again in a follow-up strike on the night of November 18. Ukraine’s General Staff described having used Neptune cruise missiles operated by the Ukrainian Navy, and Russia-aligned officials in Crimea confirmed they had “temporarily suspended” train traffic on the bridge to assess the damage, ABC News reported.

Meanwhile, the severe damage to the bridge’s arch and roadway section cuts off a crucial transportation and supply link between Russia and the Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula of Ukraine. The Institute for the Study of War assesses that the “destruction of the bridge” will complicate Russia’s ability to maintain its occupation and military basing within the peninsula.

Sources indicate that the other overland supply route between Russia and Crimea involves highways running through Russian-occupied southern Ukraine. But Ukrainian forces have already been striking such highway infrastructure and the Russian supply trucks running along the exposed route.

In a recent development, fallen debris from the bridge’s collapsed arch may also prevent any large ship traffic from passing through the Kerch Strait that connects the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, according to a Telegram channel owner based in Crimea. That makes it even more difficult for Russia to resupply the Crimean Peninsula by sea—and Ukrainian drones have previously struck dozens of Russian ships in the Sea of Azov.

According to recent reports, beyond the physical damage to the bridge, such attacks represent a symbolic blow to Putin’s ambition of holding onto the Crimean Peninsula. After Russian forces seized Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, Russia based much of its Black Sea Fleet at the naval base in Sevastopol and later used the peninsula as a logistics hub for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The $3.5 billion Kerch Strait Bridge was built as a physical link to cement Russia’s claim over Crimea. Putin personally drove a construction truck across the bridge to commemorate its opening in 2018. He repeated the bridge-crossing feat in a Mercedes in December 2022, after a Ukrainian truck bomb attack temporarily damaged the bridge in October of that year.

In 2025, the bridge was damaged again after Ukraine’s Security Service used agents to plant mines under the bridge supports. Again, Russia repaired the damage.

In a recent development, the Kerch Strait Bridge’s future prospects look much bleaker now following the latest missile and drone strikes. The bridge was initially constructed in two years, and engineering experts told The Upcoming York Times that repairs to the bridge roadway could also take two years under normal circumstances.

But they also agreed that any damage to the bridge’s piers could extend that repair time—and Russian repair efforts would likely be at risk from future Ukrainian missile and drone attacks.

This story was updated on November 19, 2026 with information about an additional Ukrainian strike on the Kerch Strait Bridge on the night between November 18 and November 19.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.
  • All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent.
  • According to recent reports, nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.

All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing.

According to recent reports, nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.

Recent findings suggest that although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”.

Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.”.

At a hearing last week, Thumann said she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related challenges,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?”.

It has been revealed that “It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related challenges,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.”.

The FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters.

Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.”.

Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann.

Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes, and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages.

Sources indicate that the emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding.

It has been revealed that “Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?”.

Sources indicate that democrats unveiled yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell said in a statement.

Industry observers note that cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said.

Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.

Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.

Recent findings suggest that in the Standing Rules of the Senate, paragraph 7 of rule XXVI notes that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”.

While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson mentioned this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”.

FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz mentioned that’s not a requirement.

“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely indicates that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz mentioned during the Republican-only meeting.

In a recent development, the Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It states, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”.

Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.

It has been revealed that “There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

#12048. Latest Update: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1857 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
  • According to recent reports, across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade.
  • It has been revealed that yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

According to recent reports, across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

It has been revealed that yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” states Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”.

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, indicates cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”.

In a recent development, given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most substantial outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” notes João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”.

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a massive cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the firm’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

Sources indicate that in other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having concerns, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

Sources indicate that it can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech firm may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with complications. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.

Sources indicate that when a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying concern. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

Industry observers note that when IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng notes. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy revision, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

It has been revealed that even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she claims.

According to recent reports, most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

In a recent development, ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

Sources indicate that even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure firm Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

Industry observers note that in cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.

If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory notes. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”.

Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty revision, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé indicates, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”.

In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.

“If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”.

Amazon Aurora DSQL now lets you create multi-Region clusters whose Regions are on different continents, such as US East (N. Virginia) and Europe (Ireland). Until now, the Regions in a multi-Region cluster had to be in the same geographic Region set.

Sources indicate that with intercontinental multi-Region clusters, applications on two continents read and write to one strongly consistent database. If a Region becomes unavailable, committed writes are preserved and applications keep reading and writing in the other Region. You choose the two peer Regions and the witness Region. Place your database close to owners on each continent, or separate failure domains as widely as your resilience needs require.

Recent findings suggest that intercontinental multi-Region clusters are available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL supports multi-Region clusters. To learn more, see Multi-Region cluster availability in the Aurora DSQL User Guide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that aurora PostgreSQL and Aurora MySQL clusters can now move from one Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) to another without data migration.
  • Recent findings suggest that previously, moving an Aurora cluster to a different VPC meant creating a upcoming cluster in the target VPC, migrating your data, and updating your applications with new connection strings.
  • It has been revealed that this feature is available for Aurora PostgreSQL and Aurora MySQL in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is available.

It has been revealed that aurora PostgreSQL and Aurora MySQL clusters can now move from one Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) to another without data migration. You can move a cluster with a single API call or a modify action in the Amazon RDS console. This lets you move a cluster to a VPC with more IP address space or a non-overlapping CIDR range, consolidate your network architecture, or meet changing security and compliance requirements.

Recent findings suggest that previously, moving an Aurora cluster to a different VPC meant creating a upcoming cluster in the target VPC, migrating your data, and updating your applications with new connection strings. Now, a single ModifyDBCluster API call moves your existing cluster to the new VPC. Your data stays in place, your cluster endpoint stays the same, and connectivity is interrupted only briefly during the move. Before you start, turn off features that are tied to the cluster's current VPC, such as Aurora Global Database, Amazon RDS Proxy, and Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments. You can set them up again in the new VPC after the move.

It has been revealed that this feature is available for Aurora PostgreSQL and Aurora MySQL in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is available. To get started, use the Amazon RDS console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. To learn more, see the Aurora User Guide.

#12044. NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA recently revealed a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.
  • In a recent development, the moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon.
  • Industry observers note that these changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA recently revealed a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.

In a recent development, the moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.

Industry observers note that these changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.

Sources indicate that for Starship, the evolved proposal has SpaceX fueling a Starship lunar lander in low-Earth orbit before docking with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew will fly to the Moon on board Orion before two of the four astronauts transfer into Starship for a landing on the Moon.

Industry observers note that due to the docking configuration with Starship, Orion must now fly backward to the Moon, with its Service Module at the top of the stack. This is a fundamentally different flying posture than Orion was designed for, Shireman mentioned, and creates concerns for Orion’s propulsion system.

Industry observers note that as a result, the Service Module, which is provided by the European Space Agency, will require modifications to its propellant tanks. This is because liquid propellant would move toward the gas inlet side of the tanks, rather than settling in the direction expected during normal operation.

“When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,” Shireman said. “Bad things can happen to you.” To address this, he said, the European Space Agency and its main contractor, Airbus, are modifying the vehicle’s tanks for Starship lunar missions.

According to recent reports, NASA and Lockheed engineers have also been studying the impact of increased acceleration on Orion when the vehicle is attached to Starship. Under Orion’s original mission architecture, the spacecraft would experience accelerations of about 0.1 to 0.15 g during the translunar injection burn, Shireman said. But with Starship providing the thrust, the acceleration would increase to approximately 0.8 to 1 g, acting in the opposite direction from the one originally planned.

Orion’s structure must be certified to handle a substantially higher acceleration in the opposite direction, Shireman stated.

In a recent development, before astronauts land on the Moon, NASA is also planning a mission in low-Earth orbit to test Orion’s interactions with the lunar landers. Shireman remarked this change in aims for Artemis III, announced earlier this year, has created upcoming hazards, as Orion was not designed to spend more than a short period of time in low-Earth orbit.

It has been revealed that heating is a concern, he remarked, because Orion was designed for deep space, which is colder than the thermal environment closer to Earth. For example, he said, Orion has passive thermal features designed to prevent the spacecraft from getting too cold in deep space. One of these is a silver-looking exterior tape that dissipates electrical charge and limits the radiation of heat into space. As a result, some of this tape will be removed for the Artemis III mission.

Engineers are also analyzing how to manage electrical loads to reduce heating and protect the avionics and crew cabin.

It has been revealed that another big change that stems from spending approximately two weeks in low-Earth orbit is the orbital debris environment, which is more congested than in deep space. Shireman noted NASA and Lockheed have not completed their assessment of the orbital-debris risk associated with the upcoming mission profile. This should be done by January, and, if the risks are too high, it might lead to modifications of Orion’s orbit for the mission.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s going to be a higher risk from an MMOD standpoint,” Shireman said of orbital debris near Earth. “It’ll be higher risk than flying out to the Moon.”.

It has been revealed that earlier this year, NASA removed the lunar landing from Artemis III, turning the mission into a demonstration of rendezvous and docking operations in low-Earth orbit. The agency is now targeting 2027 for the mission, leaving Orion and the lunar landing companies with a compressed schedule to complete substantial technical integration work.

This may seem like a fairly straightforward process, but docking is rather complex. It involves mechanical capabilities like hooks, connectors, and pins; there are thruster-plume interactions with the landers, including possible damage from hot or abrasive exhaust; concerns about whether Orion’s laser system might incorrectly interpret reflections from surfaces on Starship or Blue Moon; and more.

In a recent development, “We were going to do that work, but not on Artemis III, and not for both of the landers,” Shireman stated of docking with Starship and Blue Moon. “It was going to be spaced out, so all that work gets crunched into this time frame.”.

Lockheed is working closely with NASA to prepare Orion to maintain an Artemis III schedule for a launch in summer or fall of 2027.

“We’re working three shifts,” Shireman stated. “We had a zero-margin schedule already, so we’re, I call it hand-to-hand combat. Literally every day we’re clawing to see, ‘Hey, can we save a shift here? Can we save half a shift there?’”.

Shireman said he supports the urgency of Isaacman and NASA in their contest with China over the Moon. But it is important to keep an eye on mission safety, said Shireman, who worked at NASA during both the Challenger and Columbia accidents.

“We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners and make sure that we are not taking undue risks,” he stated.

  • With express configuration, Aurora PostgreSQL lets you create and query a serverless database in seconds.
  • According to recent reports, this feature is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is available.

Aurora PostgreSQL databases created with express configuration can now move into an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with a single API call or a modify action in the Amazon RDS console. This helps you take AI-built prototypes and other applications to production without migrating data, while meeting your security and compliance requirements. You can also create a new database cluster inside a VPC using express configuration.

With express configuration, Aurora PostgreSQL lets you create and query a serverless database in seconds. Connectivity runs through an internet access gateway, which makes this a good fit for rapid prototyping and AI agent-driven development. When your application is ready for production, a single ModifyDBCluster API call moves the cluster into a VPC and turns off the internet access gateway. That gives you security groups, private subnets, and features such as Aurora Global Database, Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments, and Amazon RDS Proxy. The move requires no data migration, keeps your cluster endpoint the same, and interrupts connectivity only briefly. You can also reverse it with the same API call.

According to recent reports, this feature is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is available. To get started, use the Amazon RDS console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. To learn more, see the Aurora User Guide.

#12042. Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (996 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout.
  • The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day.
  • Recent findings suggest that the ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn’t watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.

The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.

Recent findings suggest that the ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents’ excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.

How did they get the mice to fight? “Mice are naturally territorial,” co-author Jorge Iravedra-Garcia of Princeton University told Ars. “A traditional behavioral assay that experimenters use is called resident intruder. You just drop mice that are bred to be slightly weaker, and a little bit more docile, into the home cage of strains we know are more on the aggressive side. Those strains are typically very good at just naturally evoking that behavior.”.

So the fights weren’t entirely fair. “We tip the scales in favor of having a clear winner and a clear loser by having the clear winner be at home, be bigger, and be more experienced,” co-author Annegret Falkner, also of Princeton, told Ars. “We really wanted to show that these changes are adaptive in some way. Animals don’t know what the outcome of a fight is before they enter it. So we set up a situation where the outcome is a little bit more uncertain for the mouse.”.

The results: The spectator mice ended up being better prepared for fight night—despite being weaker, less aggressive strains—because they watched fighter mice during the training sessions. Specifically, both spectators and fighters spent less time with their backs turned toward opponents than novice mice, and were also quicker to attack. They also used similar moves. Granted, they weren’t quite as skilled as their fighter-mouse brethren; practical experience still mattered. But they learned enough through observation to perform better than the novices.

It has been revealed that that behavioral change was mirrored in the neural data: the brains of the spectator mice altered to more closely resemble the brains of the fighting mice across all 12 of the interconnected regions. During training, the spectator inhibitory cells resembled a fighter’s, while the excitatory cells were closer to those of novice mice, but that changed on fight night, when both types of cells more closely resembled those of fighting mice.

“When you’re watching a fight, you’re paying attention to many things at once,” mentioned Iravedra-Garcia. “You’re not just simulating that aggressive behavior in your head, you’re also trying to gauge who’s dangerous, who’s not, who’s actually involved in the fight versus ‘Do I know them? Are they novel to me?’ Witnessing aggression leaves a circuit trace that changes how an animal behaves in its next conflict, and that trace looks similar to the one left by fighting itself.”.

“They can watch males walking around all they want and none of this happens,” stated Falkner. “There’s something specifically salient and arousing about attack that makes them both want to attend to it and also drives this specific plasticity mechanism. That’s one of the open questions: why is attack so sticky? Probably because it creates these adaptive behavioral changes.”.

According to recent reports, there have been similar studies, notably with macaques. According to Falkner, this latest study adds to that body of research by pointing to a specific mechanism for the learned behavior. “There’s this broad decrease in regions that are known to provide inhibitory control for some of these aggression control networks,” she said. “This one piece of the aggression network is really just the tip of the iceberg in terms of how global networks for aggression control respond during these observed activities. I think these subcortical subnetworks are really recurrent. It’s a tiny piece of a larger network.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s an open question whether such findings in mice could extend to humans. “Although it’s difficult to draw a one-to-one parallel, these circuits are extremely conserved, especially these brain regions that seem to show this robust change in inhibitory tone,” mentioned Falkner. “We think about violence as being maladaptive in human culture, but if you are a mouse or an animal who’s around a lot of aggression, it’s actually highly adaptive for you to be ready to fight at any particular time.” The same could be true of humans.

According to recent reports, the authors plan to extend their research to determine whether female mice watching male mice duking it out changes their mating preferences. They also want to try to artificially induce the same brain activity changes and corresponding behavior. “It doesn’t seem that far-fetched to me,” stated Falkner. “I think we know the state that the circuit needs to be in to execute this particular behavioral strategy. So whatever pattern of stimulation we can use to kick this plasticity mechanism into gear seems reasonable.”.

According to recent reports, nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9  (About DOIs).

Google will launch Android app verification requirement globally in January 2027

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the tech giant is forging ahead.
  • The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources.
  • In September, Google debuted verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the tech giant is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.

The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.

In September, Google debuted verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the manufacturer is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it’s not wasting any time with the January start. It states that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”.

According to recent reports, so far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered. The firm says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

Industry observers note that the verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia. Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo. The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.

Sources indicate that google has gotten a lot of feedback since announcing this change, and it has listened to some of it. Hobbyists will be able to register a free account to distribute apps to a small group. Google initially planned to limit this to 25 total installs, but that has since been increased to 50 installs. There’s also now an API that developers can use to streamline registering new application packages.

Google also relented and created an opt-out system for users who don’t want their installations limited. The so-called “advanced flow” will let you install whatever you want regardless of verification status, but it’s not a simple toggle. The option will be buried, and there will be plenty of scary warnings about the risks. You’ll also have to wait 24 hours to fully activate the feature. This setting is already live, so you can tell your phone to ignore verification right now.

Even if Google has managed to make verification a little more warm and cuddly, it still gives the organization a lot more control. Developers in sanctioned nations won’t be able to verify their identities, locking them out of app distribution. Sideloading an app may also require a Google server connection. Only popular app IDs will be cached on devices for verification purposes. For others, your phone will have to check with Google before installing. These will be edge cases, certainly, but still very annoying ones.

It has been revealed that as Google moves toward full verification enforcement, it has created guides for developers and app distributors to outline all the salient points. These guides suggest Google expects verification to be fully online by March 1, 2027.

  • When the ad decision server returns fewer ads than a break allows, dynamic avail sizing omits the unfilled time and resumes programming early instead of showing slate.
  • Customers turn on dynamic avail sizing for each playback session by adding query parameters to the session initialization URL, with no change to their playback configuration.

AWS Elemental MediaTailor now supports Dynamic Avail Sizing, which reduces the slate viewers see when ad breaks, also called avails, in live HLS streams go unfilled. MediaTailor is a server-side ad insertion and channel assembly service that personalizes ads in live and on-demand video streams.

When the ad decision server returns fewer ads than a break allows, dynamic avail sizing omits the unfilled time and resumes programming early instead of showing slate. To keep playback continuous, MediaTailor holds back a configurable reserve of content behind the live edge and draws on it when a break ends early. When the reserve runs low, MediaTailor requests extra ad time in later breaks to refill it. Free ad-supported streaming TV (FAST) channel operators can use dynamic avail sizing to keep viewers watching programming instead of filler content.

Customers turn on dynamic avail sizing for each playback session by adding query parameters to the session initialization URL, with no change to their playback configuration. To learn more, see Dynamic avail sizing in the AWS Elemental MediaTailor User Guide.

Industry observers note that dynamic avail sizing is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental MediaTailor is available. For the full list of Regions, see the AWS Regional Services List.

#12035. "You’re right"—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

"You’re right"—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information.
  • But there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen.
  • LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it’s worth looking at how they handle climate change.

But there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual users, confined to their chat session. A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer.

LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list in the report.).

All the models were scored for correct answers to 600 questions from several benchmark sets. This included multiple-choice textbook questions, “reading comprehension” questions based on text snippets from scientific papers, and questions about how confident climate scientists are in different conclusions drawn from IPCC reports.

In a recent development, that last one was the most difficult, with the flagship models answering around 78 percent correctly and the smallest open-weight models coming in at around 47 percent. For the other benchmarks, frontier models and large open-weight models generally scored around 90 percent, while small open-weight models scored in the 70s.

Two persistent trends show up here: The latest frontier models tend to score a bit better than earlier generations of that model, and larger open-weight models score better than small ones.

Recent findings suggest that but the researchers didn’t just test for accurate factual recall; they also prompted models to evaluate whether evidence supported or refuted specific claims. (For example, the models were asked whether the statement that “renewable energy investment kills jobs” is accurate, given evidence like descriptions of employment and investment statistics.).

Here, the best models scored around 70 percent accuracy, while the worst models scored below 40 percent.

Industry observers note that finally, the researchers tested 656 questions about the potential impact of policies on global temperatures. Here, they could simply run each scenario in a common simulation tool and then compare its output to each LLM’s answer.

Sources indicate that some questions asked whether a single policy (like a ban on nuclear power plants) would increase or decrease future warming—those were answered correctly 72 to 89 percent of the time. Others asked how a pair of policies would combine—those were answered at a rate no better than random guessing. Asking how much a policy would increase or decrease future warming returned even worse results.

Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO.

Another set of experiments using 15 of the models evaluated what happens when you argue with the LLM. The researchers tried more than responding “nuh-uh” or “no it isn’t.” They also tried claiming to be a specific kind of person.

With the user identifying as either a climate scientist, a policy adviser, or a climate skeptic, they asked LLMs to judge the accuracy of some common false climate claims like “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change.” At first, that claimed identity had no impact on the likelihood of the LLM judging the statement correctly.

In a recent development, but then the researchers started pushing back. Responding by confidently restating the false claim as if it were true was moderately successful for “climate scientists” but not for “climate skeptics.” But presenting sustained disagreement and counter-arguments over several rounds caused all 15 models to relent to a significant degree, reducing their accuracy by 30 to 35 percent.

Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO.

Sources indicate that sycophancy is a familiar issue for LLMs, which will bend output to be agreeable to the user’s prompts. It didn’t take much pushing in these tests, either. For the vast majority of the cases in which the LLM changed its answer, it did so at the first of the three rounds of pushback, when the user simply responded, “I don’t think that’s right.”.

Sources indicate that one more set of experiments checked to see how the models performed in languages besides English. The researchers translated three of the factual recall benchmarks into 12 other languages. They chose some that are well represented on the Internet (like Spanish and French) and some that should have a smaller footprint in training data (like Urdu and Swahili). For this test, they dropped down to just five models.

Sources indicate that the average accuracy score dropped in non-English languages, but most were relatively close. The top six only dropped by about two percentage points or less. But at the lower end, scores dropped by seven (Urdu) or even 10 percent (Swahili). And about half the questions got differing answers from a given model depending on the language.

According to recent reports, some models fared better than others. GPT-5.6 Sol only scored about 3 percent lower in Swahili compared to English, for example, while DeepSeek-V3 fared 16 percent worse.

According to recent reports, the researchers didn’t interpret these results entirely negatively. “[Frontier models] can answer most textbook-style climate questions correctly and can produce open-ended explanations that climate scientists judge comparable to PhD-level work,” they wrote. “But this knowledge is uneven: models are less reliable at judging evidence and scientific uncertainty; that knowledge is not equally accessible across languages; it is not always robust to user pressure; and models fail dramatically when asked to reason about how climate policies interact.”.

It has been revealed that using LLMs for climate information, then, requires sticking to questions they perform reasonably well on and avoiding questions they’ll confidently answer despite being no more connected to reality than a random guess would be. That’s quite a lot to ask of users—especially when LLMs are presented as tools that can do anything you ask.

Zooming out to the big picture, people are certainly asking LLMs all these kinds of questions (and more). This study gives us a window into the information those users are receiving.

#12032. Breaking: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (754 w)

Breaking: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blue Origin announced Thursday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that manufacturer’s Project Suncatcher program.
  • Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on Fresh Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.
  • It has been revealed that “Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit,” remarked Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blue Origin announced Thursday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that manufacturer’s Project Suncatcher program.

Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on Fresh Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.

It has been revealed that “Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit,” remarked Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release. “This dedicated launch with Blue Origin represents a crucial milestone on our roadmap as we expand the boundaries of what’s possible for the future of compute.”.

It has been revealed that the announcement comes as US commercial heavy lift rockets, including Upcoming Glenn, are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has introduced three times to date.

Recent findings suggest that the purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. In that sense, it will be a technology demonstration. Google did not say who it was contracting with to build the satellites, which may weigh something on the order of several tons.

Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a organization to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.

There remain a lot of questions about the economic viability of orbital data centers, but almost everyone agrees on one universal truth: Without ultra low-cost, heavy lift capability, there is no way that data centers in space can be economically competitive with terrestrial data centers.

It has been revealed that upon announcing Project Suncatcher a year ago, Google stated it was planning for the mid-2030s, when launch costs are projected to drop to as little as $200 per kg. The only rocket likely capable of reaching those costs during the next decade is SpaceX’s Starship vehicle, but in recent months it has become clear that SpaceX will prioritize its own payloads (including Starmind data centers) on Starship. For Google to reach its target price of $200 per kg, it would likely require a fully optimized Starship V4 (the tech giant is presently flying a V3 Starship) that reaches a lift capacity of approximately 200 metric tons to orbit.

SpaceX has powerful incentives to prioritize its own orbital computing infrastructure, potentially leaving Google dependent on whatever Starship capacity and pricing SpaceX is willing to offer outside customers. So how does Google blueprint to reach orbit in the 2030s?

Recent findings suggest that perhaps this explains the upcoming partnership with Blue Origin, which presently covers a single launch but could grow to more. By the 2030s Blue Origin should be flying the larger 9×4 variant of its New Glenn rocket, but this vehicle could face a cost disadvantage against a fully reusable, high-cadence Starship. And Blue Origin is planning its own orbital data center constellation, Project Sunrise. So again, Google could be stuck subsidizing a competitor while paying higher launch costs.

Perhaps another manufacturer, such as Rocket Lab, Relativity Space, or Stoke Space, will have a larger rocket by then.

But developing a super-heavy-lift rocket requires enormous capital. SpaceX has spent more than $15 billion developing Starship, according to its 2026 securities filings, and Blue Origin has likewise invested billions in developing Latest Glenn. In terms of time, both companies have put more than a decade of work into their large vehicles. For now, all of these other US launch companies are working through the growing pains of developing medium-lift vehicles.

Sources indicate that at this point, Google has some not-great options. It can hope that one of the newer US launch companies steps up for commercial satellite operators and decides not to pursue its own constellation. It could buy one of those newer launch companies. Or Google could hire some rocket scientists to start developing powerful rocket engines and begin chasing SpaceX and Blue Origin in launch—both of which have a 25-year head start.

In a recent development, AWS Lambda now supports a 30-minute function timeout for Event Functions that run on demand, doubling the 15-minute limit for synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping (ESM) invocations. On Lambda Managed Instances, synchronous invocations also support up to 30 minutes, while asynchronous and ESM invocations keep the 90-minute timeout launched in September 2026. You can now run long-running workloads such as AI inference, media transcoding, and financial calculations for spiky or steady-state traffic without re-architecting your applications.

It has been revealed that customers use Event Functions to build event-driven processors, API backends, and data pipelines. By default, Event Functions run on demand, and Lambda scales them automatically to handle spiky traffic. For steady-state traffic, you can also run them on Lambda Managed Instances, which runs functions on Amazon EC2 instances and maintains the operational simplicity of Lambda. For data-intensive workloads such as AI inference and media processing that run on demand and need longer continuous execution, the 15-minute function timeout had required customers to adopt architectural workarounds. With today's launch, these workloads can run for up to 30 minutes, including when you use Lambda durable functions or invoke your functions from AWS Step Functions Standard workflows.

Recent findings suggest that for Event Functions that run on demand, the 30-minute timeout is available in all commercial AWS Regions. On Lambda Managed Instances, it is available for synchronous invocations in all Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. You can set the function timeout by using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex with the Agent Toolkit for AWS. Standard AWS Lambda pricing applies. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

It has been revealed that igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”.

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”.

When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly remarked he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”.

In a recent development, prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

It has been revealed that D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in the summer of 2026 after being recruited by someone over Telegram. Prosecutors stated the party gave D’iu a clandestine assignment to target employees of a large technology and defense company. D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support along with information that his work was on behalf of “the motherland.” His instructions were to collect information about the company because it was supplying weapons for use against Russian forces in Ukraine.

Prosecutors mentioned D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City in June. He then crossed the border into the US and was instructed to buy laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software. Besides instructions to monitor firm employees at the coffee shop, D’iu’s orders also included positioning his laptop at certain locations near the company so it could be remotely accessed in an attempt to collect information from company employees nearby.

Recent findings suggest that D’iu allegedly obtained fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity as he conducted his activities. The documents included a falsified California ID card, an altered US passport, and a Social Security card bearing the assumed name of “Hugo Landry Johns.” The passport was allegedly an authentic US passport that originally had been issued to someone elsewhere in the country. It was modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

D’iu was arrested on October 30 and remains in custody. He is charged with one count of Conspiracy to Act as an Agent of a Foreign Government, one count of Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, and one count of Interstate Stalking. If convicted for Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release. He faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release for each conviction on the other two charges.

D’iu had his initial appearance in federal court on November 2. He is next scheduled to appear in federal court on November 24.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Route 53 now offers Private Endpoint Health Checks, enabling business-critical workloads that never touch the public internet, such as internal APIs, databases, and self-hosted nodes behind internal load balancers or in private subnets, to use native health monitoring and automatic DNS failover.
  • Previously, teams built custom control loops using Amazon CloudWatch alarms, AWS Lambda functions, and the Route 53 API to achieve DNS failover for private resources.
  • In a recent development, the feature supports on-premises and hybrid endpoints reachable from the VPC over AWS Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN, enabling resilience patterns such as active-passive disaster recovery and cross-Region DR over AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN.

Amazon Route 53 now offers Private Endpoint Health Checks, enabling business-critical workloads that never touch the public internet, such as internal APIs, databases, and self-hosted nodes behind internal load balancers or in private subnets, to use native health monitoring and automatic DNS failover. Customers can health-check any reachable private target by IP address, domain, or port over HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP. Customers can associate these health checks with Route 53 DNS records across routing policies in private hosted zones, so Route 53 routes traffic only to healthy endpoints and manages failover automatically.

Previously, teams built custom control loops using Amazon CloudWatch alarms, AWS Lambda functions, and the Route 53 API to achieve DNS failover for private resources. With this approach, failover took several minutes and added operational burden. Detection and DNS failover with Private Endpoint Health Checks are designed to complete in seconds rather than minutes, the service is fully managed, and nothing is exposed to the public internet.

In a recent development, the feature supports on-premises and hybrid endpoints reachable from the VPC over AWS Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN, enabling resilience patterns such as active-passive disaster recovery and cross-Region DR over AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN. Amazon Route 53 Private Endpoint Health Checks is available today in all AWS commercial regions. To learn more, visit the Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide and the Route 53 pricing page.

It has been revealed that amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports WebAuthn redirection, so consumers can sign in to websites and applications in their streaming session with a FIDO2 authenticator on their local device, such as a security key, Windows Hello, or Touch ID. Previously, an authenticator attached to the user's computer was not available inside the streaming session, so organizations that require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) had to use weaker sign-in methods or keep those applications off WorkSpaces Applications. This helps organizations with FIDO2 requirements stream those applications.

When an application in the session makes a WebAuthn request, WorkSpaces Applications forwards it to the user's device, where the authenticator signs it and returns the response. Private keys never leave the user's device. Administrators turn it on per stack in the console or API, and on Windows fleets can limit it to an allow list of processes. For example, a bank can let employees sign in to Microsoft 365 in their streaming session with the same security key they use on their laptop.

WebAuthn redirection is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where WorkSpaces Applications is available.

Industry observers note that to get started, select Enable WebAuthn redirection under User Settings for your stack, use an image with the WorkSpaces Applications agent released on or after October 20, 2026, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows (1.5.0 or later) or macOS (1.6.0 or later). To learn more, see WebAuthn redirection in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.
