💡 Key Takeaways
  • 2026 will be the âYear of Delaysâ for data centers and AGI; it will also see accelerating AI adoption by end-consumers.
  • 2026 will be the âYear of Delaysâ for data centers and AGI; it will also see accelerating AI adoption by end-owners.
  • In a recent development, december ushers in a period of reflection in the investment world, as investors take stock of the previous year and begin to position themselves for the year to come.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

2026 will be the âYear of Delaysâ for data centers and AGI; it will also see accelerating AI adoption by end-consumers.

2026 will be the âYear of Delaysâ for data centers and AGI; it will also see accelerating AI adoption by end-owners.

In a recent development, december ushers in a period of reflection in the investment world, as investors take stock of the previous year and begin to position themselves for the year to come. This is more true than ever right now, as we seem to be in a liminal period; animal spirits have lulled, but AI companies continue to put up strong results.

My prediction for 2026 is that it will be a tale of two AIs. On the one hand, it will be a year of delays, first in data center buildouts, many of which will fall behind schedule, and second, in the AGI timeline. At the same time, AI adoption will continue its relentless rise. In 2025, startups coined the idea of a â$0 to $100Mâ club of rapidly scaling AI companies; in 2026, weâll begin to talk about the â$0 to $1Bâ club.

Entering 2026, here are the facts as I see them:.

Demand for AI CapEx from the Big Tech companies is stronger than ever.

Google and Meta are fully betting the farm on AI.

While Microsoft and Amazon pulled back slightly in 2025 relative to peers, both continue to aggressively position themselves for the AI future.

Industry observers note that supply chain players seem weary: The customerâs customer is not as healthy as theyâd wish. They are worried about being left holding the bag.

The end revenue from AI remains limited (on the order of tens of billions per year) relative to the scale of data center and energy investments (on the order of trillions over the coming five years).

There are two killer apps in AI, coding and ChatGPT. Both are expected to approach or cross double digit billions of revenue this year. Nearly a dozen more startups are on the path to cross $100M+ in the near future, across a wide variety of applications.

Significant enterprises are struggling to implement AI in-house, which is leading to fatigue and disappointment.

These countervailing forces will collide in 2026: soaring Major Tech demand will run headfirst into a supply chain that hasnât scaled fast enough to match it.

First, companies like TSMC and ASML have monopolistic positions and cannot be forced to ramp capacity. Ben Thompson has called this the âTSMC Brake,â pointing out in October that while TSMC had ramped revenues by 50% since 2022, they had only ramped CapEx by 10%. He explained further: âThere werenât too many answers from TSMC about this, which is understandable, given that they wonât announce next yearâs CapEx numbers until next quarter. What Wei did say is that TSMC was making a point to not just talk to its customers but its customersâ customers.â My prediction, especially coming off of the successful Gemini 3 launch and hype around TPUs, is that the TSMC constraint could become material in 2026.

According to recent reports, second, industrial players, which tend to be overlooked due to their fragmentation and lack of market power, may end up creating bottlenecks as data centers move into the final stages of construction. Generators and cooling units are among the most important industrial inputs to data centers, but there are dozens of such inputs; if any of these inputs are delayed, timelines would need to be pushed out. There are also labor constraints that must be factored in, as shortages in skilled labor could become a key bottleneck for completing these immense construction projects. Many AI companies share a supply base, and these industrial suppliers are faced with their own CapEx decisions (how many new factories to build). Weâll find out in 2026 to what extent theyâve sufficiently added to their own output capacity.

The average AI data center takes roughly two years to build. So if 2024 was the year of fresh project announcements, and 2025 was the year when construction investments started to hit GDP, then 2026 will either be the year where a lot of this new capacity comes online (leading to further declines in the cost of compute) or it will be the year when many of these construction projects begin to face delays. We already have seen a few of these delays publicly reported in Q4 2025. If hyperscalers begin to warehouse their new AI chips rather than installing them directly into data centers, this will be a telltale sign that the era of delays has begun.

Sources indicate that the other way in which 2026 will be the âYear of Delaysâ has to do with the AGI timeline. For a long time, Silicon Valley luminaries were forecasting the imminent emergence of AGI, with âAGI in 2027â thrown around frequently in conversation. Since June of this year, there has been a progressive walk-back of this timeline. Dwarkesh Patelâs recent podcast interviews with Richard Sutton, Andrej Karpathy, and Ilya Sutskever are a demarcating line; the new consensus is that the AGI window will be in the 2030s, at earliest. In the coming year, I expect this âupdateâ to filter outside of Silicon Valley. There are implications across many areas. The most notable risk is that hyperscaler CapEx today ends up being outdated.

Tale 2: The Relentless Drive Toward AI Adoption.

Recent findings suggest that the area where I do not expect to see any delays is in AI adoption itself. The fading of hype will have little impact on fundamentals. If anything, the best startups are growing faster than ever from $0 to $100M in revenue. In 2026, weâre going to see the emergence of a $0 to $1B club. The trend of the last three yearsâand likely for many moreâis that startups are laying the foundation for the future economy, one building block at a time. There are many excellent entrepreneurs exploring new niches, and a lot of latent value has yet to be unlocked.

Industry observers note that the best AI startups are moving with extreme efficiencyâmany are earning north of $1M in revenue per employee. This implies market pull vs. a push sale. Todayâs entrepreneurs are building âself-improvingâ companiesâthey are themselves using AI agents for functions like legal, recruiting, and salesâcreating an ecosystem flywheel effect. AI app companies are also riding a compute cost curve that should drive incremental margin improvement, especially as new data centers come online between now and 2030. Finally, with enterprises facing adoption fatigue on DIY implementations, startups are gaining even more momentum.

Industry observers note that for some, AI adoption is happening too slowly. Those expecting a rapid AI takeoff would prefer to see a deus ex machina moment carry us straight to the finish line. I think that dream is likely to disappoint. Instead, the next leg of the AI story will require hard work, creative brilliance, and endurance to reach a newly introduced threshold where AI radically transforms the economy. We need only to look at the green shootsâfounder motivation, aggressiveness, hunger to win, customer obsessionâto see that this future is coming.

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

In a recent development, netflix recently entered into a definitive agreement to buy Warner Brothers for over $82B in Enterprise Value. Itâs being called the biggest, most consequential deal in Hollywood history. The purchase comes with intellectual property including Batman, Superman, Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Big Bang Theory, The Sopranos, The Matrix, Lord of the Rings (film rights), Godzilla/MonsterVerse, Mad Max, and Mortal Kombat.

IP like this became more valuable in the internet age, and will become even more valuable in the age of AI. Earlier this year, I published an internal Sequoia memo detailing the implications of AI on the IP industry. Given the significant news, I thought it would be nice to share a few excerpts with my friends and colleagues more broadly.

On a recent work trip to Paris, a profound irony struck me at the MusÃ©e dâOrsay. The museum, a glorious former train station, is a temple to the Industrial Revolution. Its collection, spanning 1848 to 1914, chronicles the period of historyâs most rapid industrialization.

Edgar Degas: Course de Gentleman (Gentlemenâs Race).

The art is filled with tributes to this latest age: Monet paints locomotives at La Gare Saint-Lazare, smokestacks fill the background of Degasâ Course de Gentlemen, and the Traders in factory-made clothing. It is a museum drenched in the dawn of industrialization.

Claude Monet: La Gare Saint-Lazare.

This is where the paradox lies. This was the exact moment in history when the cost to reproduce a piece of art dropped precipitously. What was once near-impossible, replicating a masterpiece, became trivially cheap. Logically, as near-perfect copies became ubiquitous, the value of the âoriginalâ should have plummeted. And yet, the opposite happened. The great lesson of the dâOrsay is this: instead of becoming worthless in the age of manufacturing, these original works became priceless. As reproduction became easy, the value and allure of the original only went up.

Edgar Degas: At the Stock Exchange.

Hereâs why IP is well positioned in an AI future:.

If we have AGI, or even inexpensive content creation, that will drive down the cost of intelligence.

That affordable intelligence will be used to create an abundance of content.

Humans will react to abundance with a desire for familiarity and quality.

The value of the âoriginalâ will only increase.

In this era, âoriginalâ works will increase in value promptly.

These âoriginalsâ include art, real estate, and intellectual property.

Intellectual property that has already earned a spot in our minds will benefit disproportionately.

In the AI Era, nostalgic content will benefit disproportionately as it is manifest in countless different ways.

As content production costs approach zero, the marginal cost of fresh content will also become negligible, leading to an explosion in content volume. This content flood will profoundly shift the value of attention, the primary currency in this new landscape. Undifferentiated content will rapidly lose value, and consumers will be far less willing to invest time in new content unless itâs algorithmically recommended by dominant platforms. Very few new content concepts will break out, following an extreme Power Law.

Success in this environment will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent interest in a specific piece of content. Nostalgic content is poised to become the most valuable. In a world saturated with novelty, authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly difficult to simulate accurately; even slight deviations from the original will feel inauthentic and cheap.

According to recent reports, consumers will be willing to pay for nostalgic content due to its relatively low cost. For parents, the decision to purchase authentic nostalgic content for their children over a knockoff, especially when the real item is priced reasonably, becomes a clear choice.

The Impending Content Deluge and the Scarcity of Attention.

Sources indicate that the ubiquity of General AI will drastically reduce the marginal cost of content production, approaching zero. This will unleash an unprecedented explosion in content volume, creating a hyper-saturated information environment. In this landscape, human attention, rather than content itself, will become the primary scarce resource and the dominant currency. Undifferentiated content, easily replicable and ubiquitous, will rapidly depreciate in value. Consumers, overwhelmed by choice, will increasingly rely on algorithmic recommendations from dominant content platforms to filter and curate their experiences, leading to a profound shift in content discovery and consumption patterns.

Attention Distribution: The Fresh Competitive Moat.

Sources indicate that success in this AI-driven content economy will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent and deeply ingrained interest in a specific piece of content. This is distinct from mere algorithmic visibility, as it speaks to an intrinsic desire to engage with content. While AI can generate novel content at scale, it will struggle to replicate the nuanced emotional resonance and deeply embedded cultural references that drive genuine attention.

The Inherent Value of Authentic Nostalgic Content.

In a recent development, nostalgic content is uniquely positioned to become the most valuable asset in this future. The core arguments for its enduring value are:.

In a recent development, difficulty of Authentic Simulation: While AGI can mimic styles and tropes, accurately simulating authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly challenging. The most popular feature in Sora 2 is their âCameoâ feature, which pulls in authentic characters and people into the AI generated worlds. Even minute deviations from the original, like a slight alteration in a beloved characterâs voice, a subtle anachronism in a period piece, or a deviation in the execution of a well-known narrative, will register as âinauthenticâ or âcheapâ to a discerning audience. The emotional connection to nostalgic content is often rooted in precise, well-remembered details, making it highly resistant to imperfect algorithmic replication. This is akin to the âuncanny valleyâ in robotics, where near-human but imperfect simulations evoke discomfort rather than acceptance.

Consumer Willingness to Pay: Despite the approaching zero marginal cost of content, consumers will demonstrate a significant willingness to pay for authentic nostalgic content.

As AI democratizes content creation, the landscape will shift dramatically. The true scarcity will be human attention, and the ultimate value will reside in content that can capture and hold that attention through genuine emotional resonance. Authentic nostalgic content, by virtue of its irreplicable emotional depth and its proven ability to connect across generations, represents a highly defensible and appreciating asset in this evolving digital economy. Investors should prioritize companies that control and strategically leverage these invaluable cultural touchstones.

#11965. ‘The Hairiest 90 Minutes of My Career’: How the FAA Ground Stop Went Down

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1192 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

‘The Hairiest 90 Minutes of My Career’: How the FAA Ground Stop Went Down

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that by Wednesday of this week—six days after a 4.5-hour nationwide ground stop that panicked onlookers and scrambled air travel—US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said he still wasn’t quite sure what led to the Friday meltdown.
  • Industry observers note that still, the Federal Aviation Administration has revealed that a few things did go wrong on Friday afternoon.
  • The agency has since described the ground stop as something executed “out of an abundance of caution.” On Wednesday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford appeared to downplay the incident even as he took blame for it, calling the outage “a knee scrape, and I’m sorry.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that by Wednesday of this week—six days after a 4.5-hour nationwide ground stop that panicked onlookers and scrambled air travel—US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said he still wasn’t quite sure what led to the Friday meltdown. “The root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet,” he said after a meeting with lawmakers.

Industry observers note that still, the Federal Aviation Administration has revealed that a few things did go wrong on Friday afternoon. It involved routine infrastructure replacement, a faulty router, data overload, and disruption in some regions in the radio communications that air traffic controllers use to speak to each other and pilots.

The agency has since described the ground stop as something executed “out of an abundance of caution.” On Wednesday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford appeared to downplay the incident even as he took blame for it, calling the outage “a knee scrape, and I’m sorry.”.

While aviation industry workers maintain that flyers were safe throughout the ground stop, some felt government officials downplayed the event, which left air traffic controllers scrambling to backup frequencies even as they tried to figure out what was going on.

“That was the hairiest 90 minutes of my career,” one air traffic controller told WIRED.

Contacted for comment, FAA spokesperson Steve Kulm didn't answer questions but referred WIRED to the agency’s ground stop Q&A web page, where the agency writes it has “clear, established, standard procedures to ensure safety during incidents such as this.” It states that some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained online during the communication concerns, “allowing air traffic controllers to maintain communication with and track aircraft.”.

Here’s what we know about the ground stop so far.

To understand the communications challenges that led to the ground stop, here’s a quick overview on how air traffic control works.

Industry observers note that most flyers are familiar with the towers near airports, officially called the Airport Traffic Control Towers (ATCT). The controllers who work here manage aircraft ground movements, including takeoffs and landings. Once an aircraft gets up into the sky, around 10,000 feet, it’s passed to controllers in a Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) center, who manage airport arrivals and departures. Then, once a flight is really underway, an aircraft is passed to Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often just called Centers. There are 22 of these in the US, and controllers there guide airplanes for most of their flight, passing off the aircraft as they move between regions.

Sources indicate that the communication radios used at Centers have a range of around 150 miles—a problem when the areas they have to manage are more than 100,000 square miles each. So phone lines at the Centers lead to networks of transmitters, each installed remotely.

For decades, this network has been connected by copper telecommunications lines—outdated and sometimes brittle tech. So in 2025’s GOP-led Big Beautiful Bill, the Transportation Department received the billions of dollars in funding needed to upgrade that copper to fiber-optic cables. The upgrade swaps the system, the private communications backbone of Air Traffic Control, from one of mechanical switches to a digital system built on internet-based protocols. A contractor called L3Harris—the network owner—manages the transition, and as of last week, the project was about 70 percent complete. This was where the FAA ran into problems.

It has been revealed that the trouble began in El Dorado, Arkansas, the site of one of those remote communications facilities, which is part of the larger Center based in Memphis, Tennessee. There, the FAA indicates a contractor with L3Harris was making on Friday what is now a routine switch from that legacy copper system to a fiber-optic one. But something, it appears, went wrong when the worker plugged in a latest router as part of that transition, and the FAA still doesn’t know why.

According to recent reports, data began to flood the network, making 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to the FAA. The agency states another remote site, a radar-based facility in Amarillo, Texas, may have also flooded the network with data. To compensate, the network tried to recruit other nodes, and they got overloaded, too, taking down several radio frequencies on the network.

At first, the concern manifested as intermittent dropouts on radio frequencies at Centers in the region, from Kansas City to Chicago, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to WIRED under the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press. This made it difficult, if not impossible, for air traffic controllers to talk between Centers and with pilots through normal channels. From there, though, the complications seem to have cascaded to other regions, including the areas around Washington, DC, and Upcoming York.

Sources indicate that in control rooms—mostly Centers dealing with en route flights—air traffic controllers first noticed some “dropouts” on their radio transmissions, according to two sources. On their own, these sorts of communication disruptions aren’t unheard of. But when they began to spread to multiple regions, FAA officials really began to pay attention.

Because officials didn’t understand why the radio frequencies were unstable, the agency called a nationwide ground stop.

It has been revealed that one person who spoke with WIRED mentioned they still had access to a backup frequency during the network instability. The FAA said “some frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable.”.

Then, according to the FAA, contractors from L3 Harris blocked data from the remote Arkansas and Texas locations from the wider network. That restabilized the system, restoring radio contact between everyone in the airspace.

In a statement Friday, a spokesperson for the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, a union that represents almost 20,000 controllers, wrote that “air traffic controllers were on the job, carrying out their responsibilities and working to ensure the safety of the National Airspace System.”.

While the technical issues led to several uncomfortable hours for aviation professionals, midair passengers remained safe during the ground stop, says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San Jose State University in California. “It was certainly an abnormal situation, but it wasn’t an emergency, because we’ve trained for it,” he says. “It was not dangerous, but it was highly inconveniencing, and it was not normal.”.

Industry observers note that it helped that the radio outage did not seem to have affected all Centers, and even fewer TRACONs and local towers. That means pilots were generally in contact with controllers, especially as they circled airports and landed their planes.

It also helped that pilots don’t actually need air traffic control to fly their planes, Miller says. “Talking to a controller is not what keeps an airplane in the sky,” he says. Pilots have plenty of systems onboard that allow them to “see” what’s going on around them.

Despite the lack of clarity on what exactly happened with the newly installed router to make it malfunction, Duffy has settled on a solution: more money. On Wednesday, he officially asked Congress for $50 billion, with $30 billion of that dedicated to air traffic control modernization.

If even a small subset of these explorations make it to production, the world will be a dramatically more colorful, entertaining place.

Recent findings suggest that we are delighted to partner with co-founders Burkay Gur (Coinbase ML) and Gorkem Yurtseven (Amazon) and Head of Engineering Batuhan Taskaya (the youngest-ever Python core developer and maintainer). The team is spiky up and down the platform stack, from having one of the best kernel and compiler inference teams in the world, to nurturing model provider relationships with finesse, to grassroots devrel. Their early bet on generative media highlights up across their relationships with model providers, infrastructure performance and ability to dream with creators.

We are at the beginning of a compute explosion in generative video. As the generative media wave accelerates, fal is the inference platform powering the future of AI-first creativity. The team is growing fast to keep up with that demand, and we at Sequoia are proud to lead their Series D.

10 Best Therabody Gadgets & Theraguns to Gift This Year (2026)

📅 07 Jun 2020 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that theraguns are the gold standard for massage guns; the brand name has come to be synonymous with the entire product category, much like “Kleenex” is for tissues.
  • Sources indicate that I haven't yet tried every product in the Therabody lineup (I’m getting there), but I've put most to the test and am ready to recommend my favorites.
  • It has been revealed that need more gift ideas for the active person in your life?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that theraguns are the gold standard for massage guns; the brand name has come to be synonymous with the entire product category, much like “Kleenex” is for tissues. But Therabody, the innovative manufacturer behind Theragun, offers more than relief for sore muscles and pain. It now sells a broad repertoire of wellness gadgets aimed at alleviating ailments like eye strain, menstrual cramps, and skin puffiness (to name a few). So whether you’re shopping for a fitness lover or someone who could use a little self-care, there’s likely a Therabody gadget worth wrapping up.

Sources indicate that I haven't yet tried every product in the Therabody lineup (I’m getting there), but I've put most to the test and am ready to recommend my favorites. Plus, most are FSA/HSA-eligible and designed with USB-C charging capability.

It has been revealed that need more gift ideas for the active person in your life? Check out our guides to the Best Massage Guns, Best Massagers, and Best Compression Boots.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Theragun Prime (6th Gen) and removed discontinued products. I also confirmed up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a professional-grade massage device, the Theragun Pro Plus is one of the most advanced percussive guns on the market, incorporating vibrations, heat, and near-infrared LED therapies for an all-in-one recovery tool. It also offers cold therapy, but you'll have to purchase an additional attachment for $100 to make use of that capability—a steep add-on for what is already a splurge. After testing the attachment myself, I don't think it justifies the cost unless you are sure you'd regularly use the contrast therapy.

Priced at $650, this is the most expensive Theragun, so I'd recommend it to athletes or those who are dealing with chronic muscle pain and want the LED therapy. For casual users, some of the features might feel like overkill. For example, there's a built-in biometric sensor for heart rate tracking that I have barely used. I do, though, appreciate the OLED screen, which displays a force meter, so you can see exactly how much pressure you're applying. It's a useful function if you need a nudge to apply more pressure or a reminder to ease up.

In a recent development, the Theragun Prime (6th Gen) hits the sweet spot between the elite Pro Plus and the budget-friendly Relief. It’s still a premium percussive massage gun, with five speed settings, two attachments (a dampener and standard ball), and up to 120 minutes of battery life. You won’t get extras like heated or near-infrared LED therapy, or compatibility with Therabody’s cold and vibration attachments, but you will enjoy top-notch durability. It’s the only Theragun in the lineup rated to withstand drops from up to 10 feet, making it an excellent gift for the accident-prone person in your life.

The Theragun Relief, debuted in 2023, remains the cheapest Theragun—priced even lower than the Mini Plus. For the price tag, you’re sacrificing some of the premium features, like the LCD screen and Bluetooth connectivity to the Therabody app for device control. But you can still follow guided routines on the app, and the simple one-button control is refreshingly simple to use.

The Relief comes with three head attachments and has three speed settings, which is a step down from models that offer a standard five speeds and four or more attachments. Still, the Relief is less than half the weight of the Pro Plus, and it's equipped with the essentials, which is more than enough for the average person.

Sources indicate that the original Theragun Mini is still a solid portable device—and it's $60 less—but the Mini Plus feels like a shrunken version of the elite Pro Plus. The ergonomic triangular design lets me target trigger points and muscle groups like my hamstrings and calves with more pressure control (though, admittedly, that same shape makes it awkward to use on my lower back). Thoughtful details, like a travel lock to prevent it from powering on and a compact carrying pouch, make it easy to carry on commutes and flights.

Recent findings suggest that most notably, it brings heated percussive therapy to a travel-friendly device. The heat therapy is easily my favorite feature on the Pro Plus. The Mini Plus is also compatible with Therabody's Vibration Plus and Cold Plus attachments (both sold separately).

It has been revealed that note: Some customers have reported charging challenges, saying their units wouldn't power up, but I haven't run into any battery problems in my two weeks of testing. I'll update this review if anything shifts with long-term use.

The JetBoots Pro Plus are full-length, wireless boots that combine pneumatic compression with vibration therapy and infrared LED light. Everything is controlled from a built-in LCD screen and control panel on the lead boot, and connectivity is effortless, automatically linking when powered on.

Eight preset programs target legs, knees, and joints, but you can manually adjust pressure, intensity, and the session length. Sessions can run from 10 to 60 minutes in five-minute increments, with compression adjustable between 20 and 100 millimeters of mercury (mmHg)—a standard unit of measurement for pressure. Vibration offers three intensity levels (low, medium, and high), and the infrared LED setting is a simple on or off, with an automatic shutoff after 45 minutes.

In a recent development, inside the boots, a nonporous proprietary material reduces moisture and microbial buildup, and after months of testing, I haven't noticed any lingering odors. These are best suited for athletes, frequent travelers, or anyone managing circulation-related conditions. Conveniently for those aforementioned jet-setters, the JetBoots Pro Plus are TSA-approved for carry-on travel; just keep in mind that they're pretty hefty.

I enjoyed the original TheraFace Mask, but the upgraded TheraFace Mask Glo feels like the smarter purchase. It's easier to find (Therabody seems to be phasing out the original), costs $270 less, and is slightly lighter at 1.13 pounds versus the OG's 1.27 pounds. While the Glo has fewer LED bulbs—504 compared to 648—the difference doesn't translate to a lesser treatment. You get the same red, infrared, and blue light wavelengths, plus the signature vibration therapy that made the first-generation mask stand out.

Recent findings suggest that the vibrations are now integrated into the adjustable straps rather than the mask itself. They're usually distracting, occasionally even headache-inducing, depending on my mood. I usually skip the vibration setting altogether to make this component less irritating. Even without it, the Glo remains competitively priced among high-end LED masks.

Treatment sessions range from four to 12 minutes, and the removable eye shields are thoughtful, but I prefer taking them off to extend the light coverage to my under-eye area. I very much appreciate the cordless design, but I do miss the display stand that came with the original. I often end up storing it back in its box, which makes me less inclined to reach for it. If you, too, deal with this issue, you might consider buying a travel case for $80.

Industry observers note that I challenge you to stay awake through a full session with the SmartGoggles 2.0. I’ve been testing them for months, and more often than not, I conk out while wearing them. The combination of gentle heat, vibration, and massage therapy across my forehead, eyebrows, and temples relaxes my facial tension within minutes. I love wearing them when I have a headache from staring at screens all day, and while I don’t struggle with regular migraines, I can see them being a soothing blackout remedy in a quiet, dark room.

According to recent reports, former reviewer Medea Giordano loved the first model, and this upgrade improves the fit with contoured padding that feels similar to Therabody’s SleepMask. You still get three preset modes: Focus, Sleep, and SmartRelax. That last option uses biometric feedback to adjust vibration patterns based on your heart rate. It also syncs with the Therabody app, letting you tweak the vibration and heat intensities or incorporate sound therapy. Note, though, if you’re a side-sleeper, you’ll have to shift around, as these are most comfortable while lying flat on your back.

I’ve tested several sleep masks, and the TheraFace SleepMask is among my favorites. Many claim to be 100 percent blackout, but this one leaves me feeling totally disoriented when I wake up, with no idea what dimension I'm in—just how I like it. The contoured padding feels plush, and the adjustable strap keeps the mask in place without tugging at my hair, even when I shift around at night. It comes with a carrying case, so I always pack it for travel.

The selling point is that this mask uses vibrations—three pattern presets (Pulse, Wave, Constant)—designed to nudge your brain into deeper rest. I struggle with staying asleep, but when I wake up in the middle of the night, I just tap the button to start a 15-minute session, and it usually lulls me back to sleep. That remarked, the vibrations are almost too gentle; you barely feel them, but you can absolutely hear them. It's not as soothing as a white noise machine, so if you're a light sleeper, this might be a deal-breaker.

It has been revealed that the TheraFace Depuffing Wand has become a staple in my travel bag. It delivers both hot and cold therapy to help reduce puffiness, improve circulation, and enhance product absorption before completing your skin care routine. It’s TSA-friendly—zero awkward bag checks and counting—and ideal for tackling under-eye bags after a long flight or night. The curved applicator reaches every contour of my face, and the precision tip is great for trickier spots like under my eyes. It’s intended to be used on clean, dry skin, so I hold the opposite side of my face to prevent tugging.

The wand comes with three preset temperature levels that feel gentle but effective. While the cold function isn’t as icy as a roller fresh from the freezer, it’s consistent throughout a six-minute session and doesn’t drip. Plus, this one won’t crack if you forget to take it out of the freezer (RIP to two of my traditional rollers). An indicator light flashes at three minutes to remind you to switch sides, but this notification is easy to miss if you’re not looking straight into a mirror.

Industry observers note that cupping is an ancient healing technique that uses suction to provide muscle relief. Therabody's version combines suction, heat, and vibration therapy for localized recovery. With three levels of suction (30, 40, and 50 kilopascals, or kPa), three heat intensities (41, 43, and 45 degrees Celsius), and three vibration modes (low, high, and wave), I appreciate how you can customize the intensity of your session. The TheraCup is also programmed with an auto-shutoff after three minutes—so you don’t overdo any area—and built-in safety sensors that will cut off the pressure if it exceeds 60 kPa.

Industry observers note that theraFace Mask for $650: The TheraFace Mask is a cordless, hands-free light-therapy device that uses three wavelengths (red, infrared, and blue) to tackle different skin care goals. As a distinguishing feature from its competitors, the TheraFace Mask includes a built-in vibration therapy mode that massages pressure points around the eyes, brow line, and scalp for some added stress relief. It comes with removable eye shields and a sleek display stand, which makes it easy to store on your nightstand.

It has been revealed that jetBoots Prime for $550: Compared to the JetBoots Pro Plus, the JetBoots Prime is simple to use: You get four pressure levels (25, 50, 75, and 100 mmHg) and three durations (20, 40, or 60 minutes), all adjustable throughout your session through a built-in control panel. Th boots are wireless with a 180-minute battery life and can even be used while charging. Plus, they fold down into the included drawstring bag, making them portable and fuss-free to stow away.

Industry observers note that waveRoller for $180: Foam rollers are great for improving range of motion, increasing blood flow, and reducing muscle tension. You can buy a decent foam roller for significantly less, but with the WaveRoller, you get Therabody app integration for a personalized experience and five vibration frequencies. Designed for full-body use, it works best for warm-ups and post-workout recovery.

It has been revealed that theragun Mini (3rd Generation) for $220: I recommend the Mini if you’re new to percussive therapy or need something packable for travel. It's the smallest and lightest Theragun, with three attachments (standard ball, dampener, and thumb) and a soft-zip case that fits into a tote, gym bag, or carry-on.

Theragun Sense for $300: The Theragun Sense is slightly smaller (and lighter) than the Pro Plus, and it’s also impressively quiet. Some settings are almost silent, allowing for a discreet recovery session at any time of day without worrying about bothering your housemates. It has the same LCD screen and breathwork features as the Pro Plus, too. The main difference here is that it's compatible with fewer attachments, but four heads are still more than enough for many active individuals.

I'll be testing the ThermFace Massage ($200), the ThermNeck & Upper Back ($380), RecoveryTherm Cube ($160), and the RecoveryPulse Arm ($160).

Jake, Alex and their team are giving IT teams the power to bring AI automation from their own department to every part of the organization.

Jake, Alex and their team are giving IT teams the power to bring AI automation from their own department to every part of the organization.

Recent findings suggest that IT is one of the most critical functions inside any firm. Every employee depends on it, every system flows through it, and almost every operational challenge eventually becomes an IT problem. When IT slows down, everyone feels it: employees are blocked waiting on support, onboarding is painful, rolling out fresh tools gets bottlenecked, and entire company initiatives end up stalled.

Yet despite ITâs central role, the last decade of tooling has not truly empowered them. The powerful tools are heavy to set up and brittle to maintain; the easy-to-use tools focus on narrow use cases and deflection rather than true automation. IT teams are eager to automate and are more technical than business users. They have experimented with scripts, workflow builders, and more, but the limitations of all these tools still force them to spend the majority of their time on manual work, preventing them from focusing on higher-impact work and enabling the rest of their organizations.

Sources indicate that jake and Alex, the co-founders of Serval, experienced this firsthand at Verkada, where they led Product and Engineering and sold primarily to IT teams. They heard the same half-joking request countless times, and it wasnât about Verkadaâs products. They would ask customers, âWhat else can we build for you?â and IT leaders would reply, âCan you fix my helpdesk too?â These conversations led them to two key insights:.

The first was that true automation only works if it is faster to automate something forever than to do it manually once.

Industry observers note that the second came from watching the few IT leaders who did take the time to build automations. They would first describe the workflow in one simple sentence, then reveal a sprawling tree of branches, nodes, conditions, and edge cases. Jake and Alex wondered: what if you could actually build the entire automation the same way you describe it? What if one simple sentence truly was enough?

Sources indicate that these insights were not possible to execute on in the past. Prior generations of AI were not strong enough to make it work, which meant IT teams continued working through manual tasks. That has now changed. With modern LLMs, code generation, and reasoning capabilities, it is finally possible to build a platform where âautomate foreverâ is faster than âfix once.â.

Serval is built precisely to deliver on this, and the team is not stopping there. They are using this moment not only to build a system of automation, but to rethink the entire ITSM system of record. As our own Sequoia IT leader, Leon, shared when they chose to become a Serval customer: âServal is not AI for ITSM â it is ITSM built from AI.â.

At the heart of the platform is an AI automation engine that lets teams go from a simple sentence to a deployment-ready automation. IT can describe workflows in natural language, then refine them further â either in natural language or all the way down to code when needed. This combination of being simple enough for anyone to use, yet deep enough for the most advanced IT builders, has resonated strongly with customers. The workflows are fully explainable and traceable, with all necessary permissions included, giving IT teams complete visibility and control and eliminating hallucination risk.

It has been revealed that while their automation engine integrates with existing systems of records, Serval has also built a full-fledged ITSM platform, including a ticketing system, an access management product, an asset management solution, and more. Serval is both the system of engagement and the system of record. This gives IT a single place to build and orchestrate automations, enforce security and compliance, and capture the data that compounds their automation over time.

Sources indicate that customer feedback has been exceptional. We consistently heard how easy Serval is to use, yet how powerful, traceable, and trustworthy its automations are in practice. IT leaders described day-to-day operations being transformed â automation percentages rising every week, employee satisfaction increasing, and IT teams finally having the bandwidth to tackle projects that had been stuck on the back burner for years.

What was also exceptional, and, to be perfectly honest, not something we expected to hear at this stage:.

Many customers have already fully ripped and replaced incumbent ITSM tools and now use Serval as their system of record.

According to recent reports, automation rapidly spread beyond IT into HR, Finance, Legal, Engineering, Security, and more. In some cases, companies have churned off dedicated software vendors for some departments because they rebuilt their workflows directly in Serval.

At Sequoia, the last time we heard such customer feedback that supports the thesis of IT system of record empowering horizontal enterprise automation was 16 years ago, when we partnered with ServiceNow. That is why we were so eager to partner with Serval and preempt their Series B round.

The market thesis is one half of the story. The other half is the team. References for Jake and Alex â from managers, direct reports, and peers â were glowing. Even more importantly, those references aligned perfectly with the evidence we heard from customers and what weâve observed in talent flows. Strong talent from R&D to GTM is choosing to join Serval, whether or not they have worked with the founders before. The talent density and âpotential energyâ forming around the manufacturer are impressive and represent one of the strongest leading indicators we look for.

Empowering IT teams is an elegant and scalable way to bring AI automation to the enterprise. We are excited to partner with Jake, Alex, and the team at Serval on this journey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One afternoon in the fall of 2023—fifteen days after Hamas’ brutal October 7 attacks—the founder of the right-wing news aggregator Visegrad24, Stefan Tompson, texted a confidant to work out some private thoughts on what he called “the Israel situation.” Over the previous two weeks of carnage in the Middle East, Tompson’s team had pulled off a social media coup, and now he seemed to be wrestling with how to wield his channel’s newfound influence.

Almost from the moment Hamas paragliders first touched down in Israel, Visegrad24—then a three-year old Polish account ostensibly dedicated to “curating news, politics, current affairs, history, and culture from Central and Eastern Europe”—had managed to swoop in and dominate X’s breaking-news discussion of the war in Gaza.

Industry observers note that in the conflict’s first three days, V24’s team worked around the clock to pump out nearly 400 posts on the violence: a mix of terse news updates, soft tributes to Israeli victims, and—above all—rage-bait videos showing allegedly “pro-Hamas” demonstrations in cities across the West. According to a rapid analysis that month by media researchers at the University of Washington, those 400 posts racked up an astonishing 370 million views. As the UW researchers framed it, a 641,000-follower Polish account had just catapulted itself atop a list of “newly introduced elites” on X, momentarily trouncing the reach of legacy outlets with follower counts in the tens of millions, like CNN, The New York Times, and the BBC.

In a recent development, more to the point, Visegrad had also established itself overnight as one of the most influential pro-Israel accounts on X. And that’s what seemed to be giving Tompson pause.

It has been revealed that “With the Israel situation,” Tompson texted his colleague, “I do loathe Hamas, and it’s been the perfect excuse to show the scale of Muslim infiltration in the west” (a long-standing editorial priority for Tompson and his team). But Tompson seemed wary that Israel was already angling for a wider regional conflict. “Personally I want that war to be contained where it is,” Tompson wrote. “And the Israelis do seem to be doing some vicious things.”.

Ultimately, the founder reasoned a way through his qualms. In another message from the same day, the cigar-smoking, cravat-wearing, thirtysomething Tompson wrote to the same confidant—whom I’ll call Boris—to spell out how he’d landed with regard to V24’s “editorial line” on Israel. As Tompson saw it, V24 had been faced with “four options” once the war started:.

Sources indicate that 1. Say nothing;2. Be objective—get hated by both sides;3. Pro Muslim—there are 1.5 billion of them;4. Pro Israel—There are fewer but also they have a lot of influence and money.

In choosing between those options, Tompson laid out a blunt motivation: “My goal is to fundraise off of this,” he wrote.

Covering Gaza did fit nicely with V24’s long-standing brand of anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, Western-chauvinist content. (“The beauty of this war is that it allows us to criticize slims—especially those in Europe—without any consequences,” Tompson would later write, using a shorthand slur for Muslims.) But now he seemed to have his eyes on a bigger opportunity: using Visegrad’s “latest elite” status to rake in money from some of Israel’s most powerful supporters in Silicon Valley and beyond.

And according to an extensive trove of V24 financial records, internal communications, screenshots from group chats, and correspondence with donors, all reviewed by WIRED, Tompson promptly succeeded at exactly that.

Over the past six years, Visegrad24 has become a strangely ubiquitous force in right-wing social media, its feed a reliable kaleidoscope of dehumanized, brown-skinned aggressors and their alleged depredations against innocent, often white-skinned victims, alongside global news from a nationalist perspective. On any given day, V24 might show you a stomach-turning video of a camel being abused at a wedding in the West Bank, a parade of cell phone clips showing violent crimes being committed by alleged “migrants” all across Europe, or an interview about the Great Replacement Theory.

In a recent development, from its headquarters in Warsaw, V24’s lean pseudo-news operation has proven itself almost preternaturally adept at virality on Elon Musk’s X. It even seems to have become one of the oligarch’s own favorite accounts. For a period after November 2024, Musk became especially fixated on British far-right politics, posting nonstop about “rape gangs” of South Asian men allegedly grooming British girls. To better understand Musk’s influences at the time, WIRED partnered with the research firm Bright Data to analyze his interactions with some 30 prominent European far-right accounts over a 45-day period ending in January 2025; we found that Musk engaged with Visegrad24, a major font of “grooming gangs” content, at least three times more than any other account on the list. Another dubious mark of distinction for V24: Of all the billion-plus accounts on X, Visegrad ranks 32nd in the number of community notes—crowdsourced fact checks—that have been attached to its posts.

But in tandem with its drumbeat of demonized migrants, V24 has also excelled at capitalizing on the information wars that inevitably form around real, bloody conflicts like those in Ukraine, Gaza, and now Iran. The documents obtained by WIRED—to which Tompson responded with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer—shed an intimate light on how this playbook evolved over the course of V24’s rapid rise. They provide an unvarnished case study of life inside today’s fractured and erratic right-wing mediasphere. And they reveal how the right kind of online influence, even when it’s strategically acquired by an entity just barely above the gutter of white nationalism, can command support from some of the most powerful people in the world.

Recent findings suggest that in late November 2023, Tompson wrote to Boris with some exciting news. “Jewish VCs have created a group,” he texted. “Several. I’m in two of those groups that actively push back against founders who have supported Palestine.” In another message he described one of these encrypted text threads as “85 people. 84 Jews and me.”.

According to recent reports, “They are slowly reaching out directly … Usually they want a retweet,” he wrote to Boris. “V24 is such a massive part of the Israeli PR they all know what it is now.”.

“You’re in the belly of the beast now,” replied Boris (who requested anonymity for fear of legal retaliation).

One of the groups to which Tompson gained entry was called Jewish Alliances, described by one of its members—someone going by the handle Sean Rad, which is the name of a Tinder cofounder—as a space to “bring together Jews and non-Jews working together to fight antisemitism.”.

It has been revealed that on Jewish Alliances, Tompson came personally recommended by Shaun Maguire, a general partner at Sequoia Capital who led the firm’s investments in Elon Musk–affiliated companies. Like V24, Maguire had become vociferously pro-Israel after October 7—later explaining that the attacks galvanized him to engage in “information warfare” for the country. Maguire had even made introductions that eventually helped connect the Israel Defense Forces with Musk’s Starlink satellite communication network in the earliest days of the Gaza war. And now, on Jewish Alliances, he was throwing some weight behind V24.

“Stefan / Visegrad is an incredible account if you’re not already following,” Maguire told the group thread. Privately, Maguire told Tompson, “I’ll give u $25k and try to raise the rest.” (Maguire later told WIRED that he ultimately had to stop short of making his donation. “I would have loved to donate to Visegrad, as I think their content is excellent, but I wasn't able to for compliance reasons.”).

Industry observers note that as for the other elite group chat that Tompson states he was invited to join, it appears to have been even more rarefied. In December that year, Tompson sent Boris a screenshot of a blurb from a Puck newsletter, headlined “The In-Crowd’s Hottest Text Thread.” Tompson had circled the item in red with an arrow pointing at it.

In a recent development, “I learned this week that hundreds of the most powerful figures from Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and Hollywood have joined a sprawling, informal WhatsApp thread to share thoughts on how to build support for Israel and combat antisemitism following the attacks of October 7,” wrote media reporter Dylan Byers in the blurb. “The group, which is called Builders for Israel, includes the likes of Sheryl Sandberg, Bill Ackman, and David Marcus.”.

“And Stefan Tompson 😂,” Boris replied, to which Tompson responded with his own laughing emoji.

Recent findings suggest that on the two group chats, Tompson sometimes gawked at the proceedings, sending Boris screenshots of what he was witnessing. On November 24, one member posted the following message to the group: “I bought some domains. If anyone would like them to redirect to appropriate content lmk.”.

The member then listed out a series of five urls: “longlivetheintifada.com, wechargeyouwithgenocide.com, palestineisourhome.com, fromtherivertothesee.com, fromtheriver2theseapalestinewillbefree.com.”.

“Btw this is available albeit $75k,” the member went on, before posting a screenshot showing a listing for the domain name “Allahuakbar.com.”.

Tompson himself responded inside the group. “Oh this has so much potential! 💀” he wrote.

(A review of public web domain records indicates that all five of the first urls listed here were registered through GoDaddy using Domains by Proxy, a service that allows domain registrants to hide their personal contact information. The records show that all five were created on November 22, 2023, in two batches 33 minutes apart. It’s unclear whether anyone bought Allahuakbar.com, whose owner is also hidden behind the proxy service, but its registration record was last updated on November 28, 2023.).

As a platform for fundraising, the two group chats appear to have paid off pretty handsomely for Visegrad24. “Should have 75k on Monday,” Tompson wrote to Boris on November 18. There was $50,000 coming from “a very private man” at the Silicon Valley fintech investment firm Ribbit Capital. Ribbit's founder is Meyer “Micky” Malka, an early investor in Coinbase and promoter of crypto. Tompson would later tell Boris that Malka was allegedly planning to donate an additional $200,000. Financial records show donations of $50,000 and $200,000 roughly lining up with Tompson's messages, but Malka did not respond to requests for comment. Records indicate that Tompson also secured a $20,000 donation from the investment firm Hindenberg Research, with an additional $15,000 linked to an email address associated with the firm’s founder, the prominent Wall Street short seller Nathan Anderson. Tompson also claimed he had a “soft commitment” from the Israeli American investor Daniel Gross, a former AI lead at both Apple and Y Combinator. (Anderson did not respond to requests for comment; Gross’s representatives said they have no record of a donation.).

Notifications from GiveButter, a site Tompson used for soliciting contributions, show that other donations were linked to email addresses associated with SimpleVenue CEO Michael Sinensky, Warby Parker founder Neil Blumenthal, Wix president Nir Zohar, Lux Capital cofounder Josh Wolfe, and deep tech venture capitalist Matt Ocko.

(Sinensky and Blumenthal declined to comment, and Zohar’s representatives noted they had no record of him donating. Wolfe and Ocko neither confirmed nor denied that they’d given money to V24, but both came back with remarkably similar responses, primarily taking glitch with WIRED’s characterization of whether Visegrad is “far right.” “I don't fund or support ‘far right’ groups,” Wolfe wrote, “and thankfully Stefan and Visegard24 are pro-democracy, pro-Western values, pro-peace and prosperity.” Wrote Ocko: “Even cursory research indicates that neither Mr. Tompson, nor Visegrad24 are affiliated with or support anything other than: classical liberal Western values, including the rule of law; the defense of democratic polities from terror and autocracies … peace and prosperity for all law-abiding and civilized people; opposition to horrific antisemitism and terrorist exaltation.”).

While Tompson was fundraising away with his group-chat contacts, Boris wrote with a question. “By the way, should I take Middle Eastern money?” he asked, mentioning opportunities to raise funds from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

“100 percent yes. Play both sides,” Tompson stated. “I do the Jewish side. You do Arabs.”.

In a recent development, to receive its donations, V24 set up an organization under the 501(c)(3) umbrella called the Intermarium Foundation, headquartered in Pennsylvania but domiciled in Delaware. Over the next year and more, over a million dollars poured in. Much of the money, including some of the largest sums, appears to have come in through “donor advised funds”—“dark money” philanthropic vehicles that allow donors to hide their identities, even from the recipients of their cash. Foundation documents show that in November 2024, the organization received $175,000 from DonorsTrust, a fund closely aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, often referred to as the “dark money ATM” of the American right. Documents also suggest that V24 received $172,000 from the Giving Back Fund, which describes itself as a “national nonprofit organization that encourages and facilitates charitable giving by professional athletes, celebrities, high-net-worth individuals, existing nonprofit organizations, corporations, and others.”.

A London-born self-described “Polish South African” who was “educated in French schools,” Tompson founded Visegrad24 in early 2020. He'd moved to Warsaw from London in the mid-2010s, having worked as a PR strategist on the “Leave” side of the Brexit campaign, according to Gizmodo. Tompson’s great-grandfather, he has stated, was the Polish ambassador to England at the time of the Nazi invasion. Between the war and the communist takeover of Poland, the family was left stranded abroad for three generations. In a 2024 interview with Jewish Insider, Tompson referred to his arrival in Warsaw as his “own version of aliyah,” the Hebrew word used to describe a Jewish person’s immigration to Israel.

It has been revealed that tompson’s homecoming took place just as Poland was attempting to aggressively pattern itself after Viktor Orban’s Hungary. In 2015, the illiberal, nationalist Law and Justice Party swept Polish elections and set about packing courts, hollowing institutions, and seizing control of Polish state radio, newspapers, and television—turning the latter into nakedly xenophobic, anti-opposition, and often antisemitic propaganda organs.

With his taste for cravats and posh Barbour jackets, Tompson found an audience on Polish state TV documentaries extolling the country’s grand cultural heritage. He started a PR agency called Bracia Tompson SC, and according to the investigative site VSquare, he made short films with the support of something called the Institute for the Legacy of Polish National Thought, described by the Polish news outlet Polytka as a slush fund for the governing party.

Recent findings suggest that tompson also spent the late 2010s working on what he described as a “three-hour documentary” about his father’s ancestral home, South Africa—a country whose quality of life, Tompson claimed in a 2019 Polish radio interview, is worse today than under apartheid. The documentary project was reportedly titled African Volhynia, after an area in Central Europe where Poles suffered historic massacres, land dispossession, and ethnic cleansing—a framing that, to some observers, strongly suggests that Tompson was packaging a South African “white genocide” narrative for a Polish audience. The full documentary, however, was never released.

Instead, Tompson shifted focus to launch Visegrad24 in January 2020, with a logo closely mirroring the South African outlet News24. The name Visegrad is a reference to the Visegrad Group, an informal diplomatic bloc of four Central European nations that includes Poland and Hungary. In 2020, it was Poland’s turn to occupy the rotating presidency of the alliance—and V24 appears to have served a promotional function. When V24’s Facebook page was briefly blocked for violating community standards in 2021, the Polish deputy minister of foreign affairs spoke up for the account. “The Visegrad24 profile is not an official profile of the Visegrad Group or the Polish presidency of the Visegrad Group,” he told a Polish radio station. “However, we appreciate it for its promotion of the group’s activities.”.

It has been revealed that one of Tompson’s main partners in the enterprise was a Polish journalist named Adam Starzynski, the former proprietor of an ultra-right-wing Twitter account called @BasedPoland and reportedly a fellow board member at something called the State of Poland Foundation. Their third, more silent founder was Tompson’s brother Jan. Tompson’s sister Alexandra also became involved, sometimes serving as a de facto legal rep.

In its early years, Visegrad24 posted roughly in line with the Law and Justice Party’s priorities—positively about Poland’s abortion ban, negatively about migrants, fulsomely about Christianity and Hungarian fertility rates—and was tagged frequently by party officials, according to Polish investigative site OKO.Press.

According to recent reports, but Tompson harbored bigger ambitions, as well as some apparent personal struggles. In early 2022, Visegrad’s core team escaped the Polish winter by renting a house together in the Canary Islands—during which time Tompson was stated to be “undergoing acute drug withdrawal and was in a very vulnerable state,” according to an email later written by Alexandra and reviewed by WIRED. (In a couple of messages, Tompson refers to a time in his life when he was “on coke.”).

According to recent reports, the team had been in Gran Canaria for about a month when something momentous happened: Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine. In the early morning hours of February 24, they woke up to images of Russian tanks crossing Ukraine’s borders. They immediately began pushing out an intense volume of news and clickbait.

Bit by bit, Visegrad started gaining international traction—and international notoriety for spreading fake news. On February 25, Visegrad tweeted “PornHub cockblocks Russian users,” alleging that Russian porn seekers “were presented with a message saying the content is blocked along with a Ukrainian flag and a message of support to Ukraine”—a rumor that was debunked by Snopes and other online fact-checkers. Then, about a week later, V24 tweeted that actor Leonardo DiCaprio had donated $10 million to Ukraine in honor of his grandmother from Odesa. (DiCaprio made no such donation, and there is no evidence of such a grandmother.) Articles debunking V24’s claim promptly appeared on Snopes and CNN.

Industry observers note that this first brush with global virality came with risks. Elon Musk didn’t own Twitter yet, and content moderation was strict. “I’m really stressing out over v24,” Tompson wrote in an internal WhatsApp group named Gran Canaria. But rather than get shut down, V24 lived to see its follower count triple, growing from 80,000 to 250,000 in weeks.

V24’s boosted reach didn’t bring an end to Tompson’s frustrations, however. He appeared dissatisfied with the liberal followers that came along with being such a prominent pro-Ukrainian account. And he also seemed to be running into patronage problems: In 2022, the Polish news outlet Wiadomości revealed that the office of Polish prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki had tried to allocate about $300,000 for “the implementation of the public project titled ‘Visegrad24,’” sending money to a sports and fitness NGO called the Action-Life Foundation. Then, in 2023, according to OKO.press, Morawiecki’s office appears to have sent a bit under $600,000 for a “media center” at the Action-Life Foundation—which appeared, yet again, to be a carve-out for a V24-affiliated project. This time the grant was recalled after public outcry. (In an interview, Tompson has said he “never had a penny to run Visegrad” from the Polish state.) In October 2023, the Law & Justice Party lost its majority in parliament, ending eight years of right-wing dominance over Polish government purse strings.

Sources indicate that by that fall, Tompson seems to have realized that V24’s Canary Islands posting blitz had yielded a huge bump in influence that they’d failed to monetize. In terms of fundraising, Tompson told Boris, “we missed the boat with Ukraine.” So when V24 repeated its flood-the-zone strategy with the October 7 attacks, Tompson seemed determined not to skip the next step.

Sources indicate that by early 2024, Tompson was sitting down in Tel Aviv for a podcast interview with the American-born Israeli venture capitalist Michael Eisenberg—often billed as an informal adviser to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Less than six months had passed since October 7, and Tompson was on his way to becoming a minor celebrity among friends of Israel. “Meet the Man Who Shapes Millions of Twitter Customers’ view of Israel’s war,” ran the headline of a story in the Jewish Chronicle, which went on to describe a series of V24 videos Tompson’s team had been filming on the streets of the West Bank. “Anyone who says it is an apartheid state in Israel and the Palestinian people are subjugated should go to Ramallah,” Tompson told the news outlet. “There were Maseratis and Mercedes and a brand-new shopping mall.” As of that month, at least 28,473 Palestinians had been killed in Gaza since October 7, and at least 388 had been killed in the West Bank, Israel, and East Jerusalem, according to the United Nations.

According to recent reports, tompson was also busily fundraising. “The west is under attack,” claimed a sleek V24 donor pitch deck dated August 2024 and later reviewed by WIRED. “We face two major adversaries: radical progressives” and “nefarious States (Russia, Iran, China, Qatar).” The pitch deck called V24 “the frontier of modern journalism for western values.”.

One pitch deck promoted “Project Q,” a social media campaign against Qatar. In a single month, Project Q had delivered “97 posts about Qatar across multiple accounts,” 12 original pieces of video content, including a “viral” short featuring the British anti-Islamic activist Tommy Robinson, video essays, and an instance of then Polish MEP Michał Dworczyk condemning Qatar in a speech.

V24 also boasted that it was building “a network of Muslim and Arab influencers to push content,” including pro-Israel voices Loay Alshareef, Nuseir Yassin, Luai Ahmed, and YouTuber “Apostate Prophet,” the latter an ex-Muslim interviewee on V24’s YouTube.

Industry observers note that then there was the Project Veritas–style hidden-camera news operation Tompson had introduced, called V24 Investigations, run by the ex-Project Veritas board member Matthew Tyrmand. In the spring of 2024, V24 Investigations fanned out across American university campuses amid pro-Palestine protests to make unflattering, Project Veritas–style videos of student activists, part of a larger V24 effort to expand its YouTube presence.

But in 2025 and 2026, Visegrad would see more opportunity to draw on a traditional area of strength—breaking war news on X.

Recent findings suggest that on June 13, 2025, Israel leaped into the wider conflict that Tompson had initially been afraid of: That morning, Tel Aviv brutally ambushed Iran with an onslaught of synchronized assassinations, air raids, and drone strikes—and V24 aggressively posted through it on X. But this time, alongside its fairly typical mix of war porn and mockery of pro-Palestinian protesters, a somewhat unusual motif ran through Visegrad’s social coverage of the war: Enthusiasm for restoring the leadership of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last Shah.

Industry observers note that V24 even played a bit part in the social media war to influence US president Donald Trump as he toyed with joining Israel’s fight. On the fifth day of the war—after Trump had stated on Truth Social, “We know exactly where the so-called ‘Supreme Leader’ is hiding”—Visegrad chimed in with a post on X seemingly tailor-made to sweeten the option of regime change:.

Incoming reports of Iranian military officers seeking contact with Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi to declare their intent to defect. They also want to pledge their allegiance to His Majesty and his mission to lead the transition to democracy in Iran after the regime’s fall.

Visegrad’s post received more than a million views and was shared nearly 3,000 times.

When Trump finally did make his move four days later, dropping a set of “bunker buster” bombs on Iranian nuclear sites, V24 posted an image of the Islamic Republic’s flag being torn away to reveal that of the Pahlavi monarchy and the words “It’s time” (2.4 million views, 3,600 shares).

Industry observers note that why the outsize focus on the sexagenarian exiled son of a former dictator? Pahlavi does enjoy a certain amount of organic political support among the Iranian diaspora. But he’s also been held up at times as Israel’s preferred leader for Iran. In October 2025, Haaretz, TheMarker, and the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab reported that Israel’s government was likely behind a massive Persian-language “influence operation” to simulate online support for Pahlavi using bots, synchronized posting campaigns, and artificial intelligence—all “as part of an even broader Israeli campaign to influence the social media discourse.”.

Sources indicate that V24’s own pro-Pahlavi posting binge was underway at the same time. When asked whether V24 had received any funding from Pahlavi’s network, Tompson responded by saying, “I wasn’t aware that Reza Pahlavi was a foreign state.” When asked whether he had received any money from Israel directly, Tompson replied with an apparent joke. “Yes,” he wrote, “Benjamin Netanyahu personally hands me money for every post on Visegrad24.”.

In the three years since October 7, Visegrad24’s follower count has swelled to 2.1 million on X. But even as Musk’s platform has stubbornly remained V24’s only real area of strength, it has also become a more contested one since 2023. “They’re operating in an extremely competitive space,” says Ryan Broderick, the founder of the Garbage Day newsletter, which tracks the online media ecosystem.

In recent years, with the rise of open-source-intelligence “monitoring the situation” accounts on X—essentially breaking-news channels run by hyper-online finance people—real-time coverage of crises and conflicts has become more of a crowded market, says Broderick. Today, he figures, an October 7–style V24 posting blitz would have a harder time breaking through. At the same time, V24’s other stock and trade—xenophobic posts about migrants—is easily upstaged by countless accounts that are more nakedly, brazenly racist.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, support for Israel has only become a more isolating position to occupy on the global far right, which has leaned further and further into its natural affinity for noxious antisemitism. (In 2025, Tompson appears to have met up in Turkey with another right-wing video creator named Lord Miles—a British self-styled adventurer who denigrates many of the same ethnic groups that V24 does, only with the addition of being blatantly antisemitic. According to Lord Miles, the two were set to collaborate on a video. But then Tompson started talking about raising six-figure sums from a pro-Israel “WhatsApp group chat,” and Lord Miles bolted from the scene, later posting about the episode on X.).

It has been revealed that relatively early in its reporting on V24, WIRED reached out to some people who know Tompson, including an ex-partner. Shortly afterward, Tompson called back from her phone. “That’s not how we do things in South Africa, my friend,” he stated. “I don’t like it. I find it creepy; I find it weird.” He then offered to pay for a flight to Warsaw for an on-the-record interview with him—an offer WIRED declined, given journalistic standards against accepting money from sources. “Are you not a man, my friend?” Tompson said. “I’m very upset you have disrespected me.”.

When WIRED later got in touch to arrange a concrete date for a phone interview, Tompson asked if he could be sent questions in advance. When WIRED refused, citing standard editorial practice, Tompson balked. “Not really interested in you wasting my time old sport,” he wrote, “What exactly is the incentive for me to give you any more of my time, generosity or politeness?” He signed off the message with the words, “praying that you find Christ, who redeems all, including the likes of sinning wretches like myself.”.

In a recent development, he later turned WIRED’s reporter’s request for an interview around. “Now I am kindly offering you the opportunity to answer some questions,” he wrote. “It’s a generous offer, which will allow you to give your perspective on things and answer some notable questions about your behavior, your lifestyle, your funding, and some other details that are an important reflection of you who are as a person.” WIRED declined.

I’m often asked if Dyson products are really worth the money. As WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, I’ve tried every recent Dyson vacuum—from the newest, most powerful model to the long-favored V15 Detect—and I have a lot of thoughts on which ones you should buy, and at what price. The best time to shop is during sale season, and lucky for you, Dyson Black Friday deals have already started as of today. If you’re looking to pick up a new vacuum before your family comes over for Thanksgiving, here's the on-sale models I recommend.

In a recent development, if you want a cheaper vacuum that still comes with two cleaner heads, the older Dyson V15 Detect is also already on sale ($599), and it's even bundled with the Car Cleaning Kit, meaning three extra attachments. The V15 was our top Dyson vacuum pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still packs two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). It's a great all-around vacuum, and this bundle option gets you great extra attachments.

The PencilVac is incredibly handy and compact, and great if you're trying to do quick pickups daily on hard floors. It's incredibly lightweight and a great fit for anyone with mobility or strength concerns. If these features speak to you, this is a great time to buy, as it's already on sale.

According to recent reports, this wet floor cleaner is often on sale for around $400, so it's not a huge surprise to see this deal ahead of Black Friday. The Dyson Clean+Wash is primarily a wet floor cleaner, but it can do dry cleans, too, and does not use a filter you inevitably need to keep clean. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck noticed no weird smells in three months of use. It's similar to the Dyson WashG1, with a self-propelled design that makes it easy to push around the room, and it does a good job scrubbing floors clean. Keep in mind that it's not great for dry debris, since its just rolling, not sucking.

The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai came out earlier this year and is one of my favorite robot vacuums from the brand. That's including the newer Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV I’m currently testing, which hasn't blown me away as a better investment. It has been revealed that the Spot+Scrub Ai is much lower priced, and despite some dubious AI feature claims, it does a good job cleaning autonomously. It’s often discounted around this price, but the $400-off sale is a little better than what I saw during Prime Day.

Tech Report: 2026: This is AGI
